summary: This document defines a way to convey vendor-specific constraints in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP), so a client can ask for path computation using constraints that only certain vendors define, without a new protocol extension each time.

plainLanguage.summary: PCEP can carry standard requests for computing network paths, but vendors may need extra information that is not standardized. This RFC defines a labeled container for that information and explains when a path-computation server may ignore or reject it.

subtitle: A PCEP container for vendor-specific constraints, metrics and other path-computation data.

tldr.problem: PCEP carries standardized path constraints and metrics but has no general way to carry vendor-specific information needed by proprietary computations.
tldr.mechanism: A PCC can send a Vendor Information object or TLV containing an IANA Enterprise Number and enterprise-defined data. The object can appear in a path-computation request, while the TLV can appear in any PCEP object that supports TLVs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7470 obsoletes RFC 7150, changing the object code point and clarifying TLV use. It has been updated by RFC 9752.

today: RFC 7470 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It obsoletes RFC 7150 and has been updated by RFC 9752.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs Vendor Information
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) carries path-computation requests and responses between a client (PCC) and a path-computation element (PCE), or between cooperating PCEs. Requests can include endpoints, bandwidth constraints, metric limits and an objective function.

A vendor-specific objective function may depend on metrics or constraints that PCEP does not define. RFC 7470 provides a Vendor Information object for proprietary data and a Vendor Information TLV for placing such data inside any PCEP object that supports TLVs.

Because each vendor defines its own information, different implementations may not interoperate unless the vendors cooperate. The RFC encourages vendors to document their formats and bring broadly useful extensions to the IETF for standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP has standard fields for path requests, but a vendor may need extra constraints or metrics. This RFC defines where that vendor-specific data can be carried.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7150
sections.content:
RFC 7470 replaces RFC 7150 with two changes. It clarifies that the Vendor Information TLV can appear in any existing or future PCEP object that supports TLVs. It also assigns a different code point to the Vendor Information object.

The earlier object code point conflicted with one used in an Internet-Draft that had been deployed without an IANA allocation. The PCE working group surveyed implementations and deployments and considered the new assignment safe for early users of RFC 7150.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision clarifies where the TLV may be used and changes the object's assigned code point. The change addresses a conflict with an unassigned code point used by an Internet-Draft.

sections.title: Sending and Processing the Object
sections.content:
A PCC includes the Vendor Information object in a PCReq message to send proprietary constraints or metrics. The object contains an Enterprise Number that identifies the organization responsible for defining the data. A request may contain multiple objects with different Enterprise Numbers.

The PCE follows the object's P flag. If the flag is set, the object is mandatory: the PCE must process it or reject the request under RFC 5440. If the flag is clear, the PCE may use or ignore it. A PCE that recognizes the object but not its Enterprise Number must reject a request that marks the object as mandatory.

The object is optional in a request and can also appear in a response. It may apply to one path request or to a set of synchronized requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The P flag tells the PCE whether it must understand the vendor data. If the data is required and the PCE cannot interpret it, the PCE rejects the request.

sections.title: Behavior of Older Implementations
sections.content:
An implementation that does not recognize the Vendor Information object follows the base PCEP rules. It rejects the message if the object's P flag is set and may ignore the object if the flag is clear.

An implementation that does not recognize the Vendor Information TLV follows the base rule that unknown TLVs are ignored. A PCE that recognizes the TLV but does not support the Enterprise Number treats it as an unknown TLV. Further specifications are needed to define the position and meaning of a vendor TLV in particular PCEP objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Older PCEs reject an unfamiliar object only when the request marks it as required. They ignore an unfamiliar TLV under the base PCEP rules.

sections.title: The Shared Object and TLV Format
sections.content:
The Vendor Information object and VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV use the same body format. It begins with a 32-bit Enterprise Number assigned by IANA, followed by Enterprise-Specific Information.

The enterprise identified by the number defines the format and meaning of the remaining data. It may document that information in an Informational RFC or commercial documentation so other PCCs and PCEs can use it.

IANA assigns Object-Class 34, Object-Type 1 and TLV Type 7. The previous object value 32 is marked Unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The format starts with a 32-bit number that identifies the organization. The organization defines the meaning and format of the data that follows.

sections.title: Configuration and Network Effects
sections.content:
A PCC may make vendor information configurable across the whole client, per PCE or per request. A PCE may configure whether it supports the information and which policies govern its use. Standard MIB modules should not expose detailed vendor content, though they may report use of the object or TLV and the Enterprise Numbers seen.

Unsupported data can increase PCEP message size and consume bandwidth and processing. A PCC should monitor PCE capabilities and should not send vendor information to a PCE it believes cannot process it or forward the request to a capable PCE. Advertising supported Enterprise Numbers is outside this RFC's scope.

The extensions do not substantially change PCEP security. The base PCEP protections apply, and authentication and integrity mechanisms can help defend against oversized messages intended to consume resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should send vendor data only to PCEs that can handle it. Large unsupported messages can waste network capacity and processing time.
